title: Latest Row Per Group Without a Sort
description: The 'latest row per group' query sorts the whole table; an index matching the window's partition and order does it with no Sort. Why it matters: "latest per customer/account/entity" is one of the most frequently needed query patterns in business software, and doing it efficiently at scale is a genuinely valuable skill.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About
'Show me the most recent order for each customer' — or the latest login per user, the newest support ticket per account, the current price per product — is one of the single most common query patterns in business software, generally known as **top-N-per-group** (here, top-1-per-group specifically: just the single latest row for each group). It comes up constantly because almost every real system has some notion of 'entities' (customers, accounts, products) each with a history of related records, and dashboards nearly always want to show 'the latest thing that happened' per entity rather than the entire history.

The standard modern way to express this in T-SQL is a window function wrapped in a filter: number each customer's orders from newest to oldest with `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY CustomerId ORDER BY OrderDate DESC)`, then keep only the rows where that number equals 1. Conceptually this is exactly right and reads clearly: 'group by customer, sort each group newest-first, keep #1 from each group.' The trap, though, is entirely about *how* SQL Server has to produce that numbering, and it's the same underlying mechanism covered in this course's window-function-and-sort lesson, just applied to a slightly different, extremely common business scenario, so it's worth seeing it a second time in this specific shape.

To assign row number 1, 2, 3... within each customer ordered by date, SQL Server has to see all of a customer's rows arrive together, and within that group, in newest-first order. If nothing about the table's physical storage already presents rows in that shape — and by default, a table's clustered index is very likely ordered by something else entirely, like `OrderId` — SQL Server has no choice but to read every single row in the table, dump them into a working area, and perform an explicit **Sort** to arrange them into `(CustomerId, OrderDate DESC)` order before it can even begin numbering anything. Picture a huge box of receipts from every customer all mixed together, and being asked to find just the single most recent receipt for each customer: the reliable way to do that by hand is to first sort the whole box by customer and then by date within each customer, and only then can you walk through and pick off the top one per group. That full sort happens regardless of the fact that, in the end, you're only going to keep one row out of every customer's whole history and discard the rest — the Sort has to process every row before it can produce even its first output row, because it can't know whether a later row belongs earlier in the sort order until it's actually seen the whole input.

For 300,000 orders, that means SQL Server does a large, memory-hungry (and, on a poorly-estimated grant, potentially tempdb-spilling) sort of the *entire table*, purely to answer a question whose actual output is only one row per customer. If there are, say, 5,000 distinct customers, you're paying the cost of fully sorting 300,000 rows in order to keep just 5,000 of them — a huge amount of wasted sorting work relative to what actually survives the filter.

The fix, once again, doesn't touch the query's logic at all — it's purely about supplying an index that already presents the data in the shape the window function needs. If you build an index keyed on `(CustomerId, OrderDate DESC)`, the index itself is physically stored grouped by customer, and within each customer's group, ordered newest-to-oldest — exactly matching the window's `PARTITION BY CustomerId ORDER BY OrderDate DESC` specification. SQL Server's optimizer recognizes this match and can simply walk the index in the order it's already stored, assigning row numbers as it streams past, with **no Sort operator required at all**. Because the index also naturally groups each customer's rows together with the newest one first, the engine can, in many cases, even stop early once it's produced the first row per customer group and move on to the next customer, rather than processing every historical row for every customer in full.

What to look for when diagnosing this in an execution plan: a **Sort** operator sitting over a scan of the full table, feeding into the window-function machinery (shown as **Sequence Project** and **Segment**, or similar operators depending on version), with the total rows processed by the Sort matching the *entire* table size rather than anything close to the small number of rows the query actually returns. That mismatch — full-table Sort cost for a query that keeps one row per group — is the signature of this exact pattern, and matching an index's key columns to the window's `PARTITION BY` (first) and `ORDER BY` (second) is the reliable, repeatable fix for it, regardless of which specific 'latest per group' business scenario you're solving.

## Scenario
A dashboard needs each customer's **most recent** order — the classic "latest row per group." The query numbers rows within each customer by date and keeps number 1. Over 300,000 orders it sorts the entire table first.

## Why it's slow
`ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY CustomerId ORDER BY OrderDate DESC)` must present the rows grouped by customer and ordered by date. With no matching index, SQL Server reads the whole table and performs a big **Sort** to produce that order before it can assign row numbers and filter to `rn = 1`.

## What to look for
- A **Sort** operator over the full table feeding the row-number computation (Sequence Project / Segment).
- Work proportional to all rows, though only one row per customer survives.

## The concept
Give the window its ordering for free. An index keyed on **`(CustomerId, OrderDate DESC)`** already stores rows grouped by customer and newest-first within each — exactly what the window needs. The optimizer reads it in order and assigns row numbers with **no Sort**. Matching the index to the window's `PARTITION BY` + `ORDER BY` is the key to fast top-N-per-group queries.
startingQuery:
WITH Ranked AS (
    SELECT OrderId, CustomerId, OrderDate, Total,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY CustomerId ORDER BY OrderDate DESC) AS rn
    FROM Orders
)
SELECT CustomerId, OrderId, OrderDate, Total
FROM Ranked
WHERE rn = 1;
hints: The window has to order 300,000 rows by (CustomerId, OrderDate) and there's no index for it, so it Sorts.
An index whose key matches the PARTITION BY then ORDER BY of the window supplies that order with no Sort.
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Orders_Cust_Date ON Orders(CustomerId, OrderDate DESC) INCLUDE (Total); then re-run.
